title: Basic Statistics
text:
Measures of center
Often we want to know the average of some data.
There are three common ways of doing this.
mean - sum of all values divided by the number of values.
median - the number in the middle of the values.
mode - the most common number.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
The data
Let’s make some data. Pretend I went out and asked 4 people who live in Holyoke, MA their salary. Below is a summary of the answers:

fictional annual salaries from 4 people


person
salary




1
40000


2
50000


3
60000


4
1000000



To bring these salaries into R we can create a vector with the c() function, and save it to a variable called salaries

salaries = c(40000,50000,60000,1000000)

title: Basic Statistics
text:
Mean of the Data
We can find the mean of the data with the mean() function.

mean(salaries)

[1] 287500


In this case r adds up the values and divides by 4.
The mean of the data, in this case, is not a good representation of the people surveyed.
The mean is sensitive to outliers.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
Median of the Data
To find the median we use the median() function.

median(salaries)

[1] 55000


In this case R finds the number in the middle of the 4. Note there is no number exactly in the middle so R finds the mean of the two closest to the middle (50,000 and 60,000).
In this case the median is a better representation of most of the people we surveyed.
The Median is not sensitive to outliers.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
The Mode
There is no mode function in R, and usually we find the mode just by inspection of the data. We can use the table() function for this.

table(salaries)

salaries
40000 50000 60000 1e+06 
    1     1     1     1 


We can see this data has no mode.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
Sample size
The sample size of our data is the number of observations made. An observation in this case is a person’s salary. For our data above the sample size is 4.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
Population size
The population is the total size of the thing you are studying. So the population of the salary data may be everyone that lives and earns a salary in Holyoke, MA.

title: Basic Statistics
text:
Measures of Spread
There are two measures of spread that I’ll mention from time to time in this course.
Inner Quartile Range. This is the width between 25% and 75% of the data. We can find it with the IQR() function
Standard Deviation. This is the average distance from the mean of the data. We calculate it with the sd() function.
We’ll discuss these two more as they come up in the course.

Goal: Communication
Remember the goal of making data graphics to to communicate some idea.
In this lecture we’ll talk about different color palettes and when to use them.
We’ll use the penguins data again.

title: Color Theory
text:
The two functions
The two functions we’ll use for colors are
scale_*_brewer() scale_*_distiller()
The * matches the aestheic we are trying to color.

scale_fill_brewer()     #<- filling discrete

scale_fill_distiller()  #<- filling continuous

scale_color_brewer()

scale_color_distiller()

title: Color Theory
text:
Base Graph
Below is a scatter plot of body_mass_g vs bill_depth_mm.


Code
penguins |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(x=body_mass_g,bill_depth_mm))

title: Color Theory
text:
Sequential 1
I’d like to show the flipper length as a third variable. flipper_length_mm is a continuous and numeric variable. We can color by it.


Code
penguins |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = body_mass_g, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    color = flipper_length_mm))

title: Color Theory
text:
Sequential 2
The lighter color should indicate less.
To reverse it I’ll add scale_color_distiller(direction = 1) because we’re working with a continuous variable and we’re coloring.


Code
penguins |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = body_mass_g, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    color = flipper_length_mm))+
  scale_color_distiller(direction = 1)

title: Color Theory
text:
Sequential 3
Using the default color isn’t great. Let’s choose a premade brewer palette.
To reverse it I’ll add scale_color_distiller(direction = 1) because we’re working with a continuous variable and we’re coloring.


Code
penguins |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = body_mass_g, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    color = flipper_length_mm))+
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "Greys",  direction = 1)

text:
Sequential
Notes:

title: Color Theory
text:
Diverging Palettes
If we want to use two base colors, one to show high values and the other to show low. We can use a diverging palette.
Here the brown is long flipper and dark blue is short flipper.


Code
penguins |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = body_mass_g, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    color = flipper_length_mm))+
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "BrBG")

title: Color Theory
text:
Diverging Palettes 2
It often makes more sense to use a diverging palette with the middle being zero.
Here I do a bit of wrangling to add a new column, which captures the difference from the average height.


Code
ave_mass = mean(penguins$body_mass_g,na.rm = TRUE)

penguins |>
  mutate(diff_mass_from_avg =body_mass_g - ave_mass)|>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = flipper_length_mm, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    color = diff_mass_from_avg))+
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "BrBG")

title: Color Theory
text:
Diverging Palettes 3
I’m adding a circle around each point so they are easier to see.


Code
ave_mass = mean(penguins$body_mass_g,na.rm = TRUE)

penguins |>
  mutate(diff_mass_from_avg =body_mass_g - ave_mass)|>
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(aes(
    x = flipper_length_mm, 
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    fill = diff_mass_from_avg,
    ),
    shape = 21,   # <- this is a circle that allows outlining
    color = "black",  # <- outline color
    stroke = 0.3,    # <- outline thickness
    size = 3)+
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "BrBG")

title: Color Theory
text:
Diverging Palettes 4
Missing Data should be clearly represented with grey or a like color.

#Make Mass Median Income

    ))

title: Joins
text:
bind_cols()
This function just smashes two dataframes together.
Only use if you are sure that the rows match up together.

bind_cols( band_instruments, band_members)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  name...1 plays  name...3 band   
  <chr>    <chr>  <chr>    <chr>  
1 John     guitar Mick     Stones 
2 Paul     bass   John     Beatles
3 Keith    guitar Paul     Beatles

title: Joins
text:
full_join()
Keeps all the data and by default matches by a column name.

full_join(band_instruments, band_members)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  name  plays  band   
  <chr> <chr>  <chr>  
1 John  guitar Beatles
2 Paul  bass   Beatles
3 Keith guitar <NA>   
4 Mick  <NA>   Stones

title: Joins
text:
left_join()
Keeps all data in the left dataframe, adding rows from the right dataframe if there is a key match.

left_join(band_instruments, band_members)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name  plays  band   
  <chr> <chr>  <chr>  
1 John  guitar Beatles
2 Paul  bass   Beatles
3 Keith guitar <NA>

title: Joins
text:
inner_join()
Keeps only the data when keys match in both data frames. This is helpful when you want to know what values the dataframes have in common.

inner_join(band_instruments, band_members)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  name  plays  band   
  <chr> <chr>  <chr>  
1 John  guitar Beatles
2 Paul  bass   Beatles

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
The Data
In this lecture I’ll use one set of data called palmerpenguins to illustrate some of the ideas you should consider when building a graph.
We’ll focus mostly on the numeric variables in this lecture, although many of the ideas are similar for both numeric and categorical variables.

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
Example mass
Recall how we can use summarize from lab 2 to calculate descriptive statistics.

# Putting inside of summarize is helpful
penguins |> 
  summarize(
    body_mass = mean( body_mass_g, na.rm=TRUE)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  body_mass
      <dbl>
1     4202.


Below we can calculate the mean() with base R (i.e. without summarize()).

# But not necessary

mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 4201.754

text:

To find the median flipper length using summarize() you would use this code in a chunk:

# Putting inside of summarize is helpful
penguins |>

)

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
Boxplots
Boxplots are helpful for finding outliers.
Try to make a boxplot of the penguins bill_depth_mm color it by island.

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
Code for graph

## boxplot for bill depth, separated by island.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_depth_mm, color = island))+
  geom_boxplot()

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
geom_vline()
If you want to mark part of the graph, sometimes a vertical line is helpful. You simply add on a geom_vline() layer.

# Adding a brown line to show the mean billdepth. 

mean_bill_depth = mean(penguins$bill_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_depth_mm, color = island))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean_bill_depth,
    color="brown",
    linetype="dashed")

title: Taxonomy of Graphs part 2: Numeric Data
text:
faceted
We can break code into smaller piece called facets.

# In the code below I am faceting by species

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_depth_mm, color = island))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(
      penguins$bill_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    color="brown",
    linetype="dashed")+
  facet_grid(~species)

title: Notes On Style
text:
1. files names
I will use underscores _, not spaces to name your files. You can also use -

Avoid special symbols.
Called snake case.

good name
my_file.qmd
poor name
my file!.qmd

title: Notes On Style
text:
2. Syntax
syntax is how the code looks

variables should be in snake case and lower case
variables should be nouns
functions should be verbs (functions is an optional topic)
names should be meaningful and concise.
Don’t reuse built in R names (TRUE, mean, c, n, etc. )


# good
first_name = "Nic" 

# nmean is a built in function and should not be overwritten
mean = "Schwab"

title: Notes On Style
text:
<- or =
The R community likes to use the <- for variable assignment. However in most other languages = is used, and it works in R.
I will generally use = in this course. For us they are effectly the same.

first_name = "Nic"
# same as 
first_name <- "Nic"

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Data
When building graphs with the tidyverse we want the data to be a dataframe. You can use the class() function to determine if a data file is a dataframe.

library(tidyverse)
#install.packages(mdsr)
library(mdsr)
# In OO class() returns the object type. 
class(iris)

[1] "data.frame"


In this class if a data set is not a data frame (or a tibble) we’ll turn it into one.

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Variables
We want to know the variable type (numeric or categorical) we are working with so we can choose the best graph for it.
You can see this by viewing the data.

head(MLB_teams, 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 11
  yearID teamID lgID      W     L  WPct attendance normAttend  payroll metroPop
   <int> <chr>  <fct> <int> <int> <dbl>      <int>      <dbl>    <int>    <dbl>
1   2008 ARI    NL       82    80 0.506    2509924      0.584 66202712  4489109
# ℹ 1 more variable: name <chr>


In general:

integers (int) and floats (dbl) are numeric
strings (chr) and factors (fct) are categorical

However sometime integers can be categorical, and strings can be numeric. We’ll address these situations as they arrise.

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Asthetics
Asthetics are the graph features you want to map to your graph. They are often:

x
y
fill
color
shape

title: Options when building a graph
text:
the pipe |>
The pipe |> is a common r operator that improves code readability. It mean up this into the first argument of that function.
We generally pipe our data into ggplot() when graphing.
Note that metroPop is a numeric variable, and should be graphed with a histogram.

MLB_teams |>   # <- this is the data
    ggplot() +  # <- this is what we are doing
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop ) )  # <- This is our asthetic

title: Options when building a graph
text:
We can change aes()
Using the code above we can easily change aesthetics.

MLB_teams |>   # <- this is the data
    ggplot() +  # <- this is what we are doing
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = payroll ) )  # <- This is our asthetic{r}

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Sidenote: scientific notation
We can drop the scientific notation with scale_x_continuous() function.


Code
MLB_teams |>   # <- this is the data
    ggplot() +  # <- this is what we are doing
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop ) ) + # <- This is our asthetic
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Faceting
We can also facet our data to make separate plots of features. We have to tell R which variable we want to facet by, I’ll do lgID for league.
Now our x-axis numbers are jumbled. We’ll fix that on the next slide.


Code
MLB_teams |>   
    ggplot() + 
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop ) ) + 
    facet_wrap(~lgID) +  # <--  wrap by league
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Sidenote 2: fixing axes numbers
We can abbreviate the axis numbers in a variety of ways. I had to look this one up, because I don’t use it often.


Code
library(scales) # need this to use cut_short_scale()
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop ) ) + 
    facet_wrap(~lgID) +
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() )
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Adjusting alpha
Instead of faceting we can leave the graphs on the same axes but adjust the transparency. alpha is not an aesthetic, but a parameter like mapping. Note: as our lines get longer we break them up.


Code
library(scales) # need this to use cut_short_scale()
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5     # <- Alpha is outside aes()
                  ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() )
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Stacked
By default R stacks our plots ( and pick gross colors) This make the American League look taller than the National League. We should dodge them instead by setting the position parameter.


Code
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5,
                   position = "dodge"
                  ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() ),
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
bin width and bins
Each geom has its own parameters. we can adjust the bin width parameter of geom_histogram() so our bars are not so skinny. We can also specify the exact bins with the bins parameter.


Code
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_histogram( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5,
                   position = "dodge",
                   #binwidth = 1000000
                   bins = 10
                   
                  ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() ),
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
Changing geom
Once you have your graph, you may want to change the geom to try other visual representations of your data. You can easily do this. Let’s change geom_histogram to geom_density(). We get a warning about bins and position, because those are not parameters of geom_density.


Code
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_density( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5,
                   position = "dodge",
                   #binwidth = 1000000
                   bins = 10
                   
                  ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() ),
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
geom_density()
geom_density() shows the proportion of your data out of 100.You can change the y-scale to get a better image of what I mean.


Code
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_density( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5,
                   position = "dodge",
                   #binwidth = 1000000
                   bins = 10
                   
                  ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() ),
    )+
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = label_number(labels = scales::label_comma() )
    )

title: Options when building a graph
text:
legend
You can adjust the legend name too.


Code
MLB_teams |>  
    ggplot() +  
    geom_density( mapping = aes( x = metroPop,
                                 fill = lgID,
                                 ),
                   alpha = 0.5,
                    ) + 
    
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale() ),
    )+
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = label_number(labels = scales::label_comma() )
    )+
    labs(fill ="League ID")+
    scale_fill_manual(labels = c("American League", "National League"),
                     values = c("blue","red"))

Importing a .csv file.
A .csv file is a special type of text document. csv is short for “comma separated values.” Essentially its a text file with commas separating the data within the file.
There are other ways of separating data (such as with tabs).
The tidyverse has a function called read_csv() which will take a .csv file and read it into memory so you can use it.

Exercise
Use the tidycensus package to conduct a spatial analysis of the American Community Survey data it contains for Massachusetts. Answer the question: Which counties in Massachusetts have the highest proportion of retirees (Use age > 65 as a proxyt for retirement)?
Instructions for using the tidycensus package

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

# Write your code below
mass_prop_retirees <- 
  tidycensus::get_acs(
    geography = "county", 
    variables = c(population = "B01003_001",age_1="B01001_044", age_2='B01001_045', age_3='B01001_046',age_4='B01001_047', age_5 = 'B01001_048', age_6 = 'B01001_044'),
    state = "MA",
    geometry = FALSE
  ) |>
  # Add centroids to each region using purrr package
 tidyr::separate(NAME, c("County", "State"), sep = ", ") |> 
 tidyr::separate(County, c("County", "Fluff"), sep = " ") 

mass_prop_retirees <- mass_prop_retirees |> 
  select(County,variable,estimate)|>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(proportion = (age_1+age_2+age_3+age_4+age_5)/population)

# Do a left join, a right join will lose the multipolygon-ness
mass_prop <- mass_pop |>
  left_join(mass_prop_retirees, by = "County")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mass_prop, aes(fill = proportion)) +
  scale_fill_distiller(direction = 1)
